blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights this paper as an insightful analysis of BoPETs (Build-On-Property-revealing-EncrypTion) systems, which aim to enable cloud services to operate on encrypted data while preserving privacy. The paper critiques the current state of BoPETs, using the Mylar system (built on Meteor.js) as a case study to demonstrate both their potential and limitations. Key takeaways include the dangers of assuming security against snapshot passive adversaries when deploying systems against active adversaries, the exposure of metadata even in seemingly secure systems, and the need for realistic threat models and formal cryptographic definitions. The paper also provides practical lessons from porting real-world applications to BoPETs, revealing the subtle and critical decisions required in access control and encryption strategies. The authors emphasize that security proofs must be carefully contextualized, as real-world deployments often violate implicit assumptions.
paper_title: Breaking Web Applications Built on Top of Encrypted Data
paper_abstract: We develop a systematic approach for analyzing client-server applications that aim to hide sensitive user data from untrusted servers. We then apply it to Mylar, a framework that uses multi-key searchable encryption (MKSE) to build Web applications on top of encrypted data. We demonstrate that (1) the Popa-Zeldovich model for MKSE does not imply security against either passive or active attacks; (2) Mylar-based Web applications reveal users’ data and queries to passive and active adversarial servers; and (3) Mylar is generically insecure against active attacks due to system design flaws. Our results show that the problem of securing client-server applications against actively malicious servers is challenging and still unsolved. We conclude with general lessons for the designers of systems that rely on property-preserving or searchable encryption to protect data from untrusted servers.
